## Instructions

- This is a closed-book, closed-notes exam. No reference sheet, computer, phone, calculator, smartwatch, or other electronic device is permitted.

- You must work independently and may not communicate with any other person during the exam.

- Show your reasoning. Exact formulas, setup, and interpretations receive credit even when an arithmetic calculation is not completed.


\newpage

1. (11pt) Suppose the probability mass function of a discrete random variable $X$ is given by: 

    $P(X=0.1) = a$, $P(X=0.2) = b$, $P(X=0.3) = c$

(1) For each of the following statement, specify if it's True or False.

    (T/F) The values of a, b, and c must be between 0 and 1. 
 
    (T/F) The values of a, b, and c must satisfy that $a+b+c=1$.
 
    (T/F) The values of a, b, and c must all be 1/3.
 
    (T/F) This is not a valid probability mass function since 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 do not add up to 1.

\vspace{6pt}
(2) If you are asked to "simulate from the distribution of X for a large number of times," what could your result look like?  Choose one.

    (i) 0.1
    (ii) a, b, a, a, b, c, ......
    (iii) 0.1, 0.3, 0.1, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, ......
    (iv) 1, 3, 3, 1, 2, 3, .....



\vspace{10pt}

2. (8pt) There is a $2\%$ click rate for an online advertisement, and we decide to use a binomial model to study people's clicking behavior of the advertisement.

(1) The following are five random draws from a binomial distribution with parameters $p=0.02$ and $n=100$: $0, 3, 1, 1, 2.$  What do these numbers represent in this context?  Choose one.

    (i) We have simulated five people.  The first simulated person clicks no advertisement, the second simulated person clicks 3 advertisements, etc.
    (ii) We have simulated five people. The first simulated person clicks the advertisement 0 times, the second simulated person clicks the advertisement 3 times, etc.
    (iii) In one simulation, 0 out of 100 people click the advertisement; in another simulation, 3 out of 100 people click the advertisement, etc.
    (iv) We simulate the behavior of one person.  The simulated person clicks the advertisement 0 times, and then 3 times, and then 1 time, and then 1 time, and then 2 times.



(2) Suppose you are a statistical consultant and your client told you the following things.  Which of these would make you concerned about the assumptions of the binomial model?  Choose one.

    (i) "We want to focus our research on how females react to the advertisement and we did not include any males in our random sample."
    (ii) "The advertisement was only sent to 20 people."
    (iii) "We send the advertisement to people with the same IP address, so some people in our sample might be from the same household."
    (iv) "The click rate for this advertisement has always been very low."


(3) For your choice in (2), briefly explain which model assumption might be violated.


\newpage

3. (4pt) You play a game with me as follows. A fair coin is tossed. If a head shows up, I give you a dollar. If a tail shows up, you give me a dollar. You want to study the distribution of your net winning if you play the game for 10 times. Which of the following is the most appropriate simulation plan?  Choose one.

    (i) Simulate a very long sequence of H and T's, like H, H, T, H, T, ..., where H and T occur equally likely.  Calculate the net winning based on the outcome.
    (ii) Simulate a sequence of 10 H and T's, where H and T occur equally likely.  Calculate the net winning based on the outcome.  Repeat for a large number of times, recording the net winning each time.
    (iii) Randomly draw one H or T with equal probability.  Record if you win a dollar or lose a dollar accordingly.  Repeat for a large number of times, recording the result (+$1 or -$1) each time.
    (iv) Simulate a sequence of 0's and 1's, where 0 represents Tail and 1 represents Head.  Repeat for 10 times and calculate the sum of the 10 numbers.

\vspace{10pt}

4. (10pt) On any Friday night between 6pm and 7pm, there are, on average, 3 cars per minute driving past a certain traffic light. We model the exact number of cars driving past the traffic light with a Poisson distribution.

(1) What are the **two** assumptions of the Poisson model **in the context of this problem**? Describe a scenario that might make the assumptions invalid.

\vspace{100pt}

(2) What is the probability that exactly 20 cars will drive past the traffic light during a 5-minute interval? Set up the probability expression and evaluate it if possible.

\vspace{50pt}

(3) What is the probability that 20 or more cars will drive past the traffic light during a 5-minute interval? Write the probability in terms of the Poisson cumulative distribution function and explain how you would calculate it.

\vspace{50pt}


\newpage

5. (15pt) Suppose among adult customers visiting a flower shop on Valentine's Day, $72\%$ made a purchase.

(1) What is the probability that, out of 10 customers visiting on Valentine's Day, exactly 9 make a purchase? Set up the binomial probability formula and evaluate it if possible.

\vspace{50pt}

(2) What is the probability that the 10th customer visiting on Valentine's Day is the 2nd person to not make a purchase? Identify the appropriate distribution and write the probability expression.

\vspace{50pt}

(3) How many customers would have to visit on Valentine's Day to have more than a $95\%$ chance of at least 20 purchases? (Hint: the answer is a number between 30 and 40.) Explain how you would determine the smallest such number.

\vspace{50pt}

(4) For any model you have used for (1), (2), or (3) above, pick *one* required assumption and discuss its validity *in context*.  For instance, describe a scenario that could violate this assumption, or a scenario that could make the assumption more valid.

\vspace{110pt}


6. (12pt) For each of the following scenarios, name the most appropriate distribution to model $X$ and specify the corresponding parameter values (e.g., "binomial distribution with parameters $n=10$ and $p=0.5$").

(1) Suppose you get spam emails at a constant rate of 8 emails per day.  Let X be the number of spam emails you will get in the next 12 hours.

\vspace{30pt}

(2) I can make a free throw 28% of the time when I play basketball.  Let X be the number of free throw attempts when I make my fifth free throw.

\vspace{30pt}

(3) Among 20 patients that have a certain disease with a recovery rate of 96%, X is the number of them that will recover.



\newpage

7. (20pt) Suppose you play a gambling game as follows. A fair coin is flipped continuously. Every time you see a head, you win $\$1$. The game stops when you see the first two consecutive tails. The results of 10 games are given below (1 represents head and 0 represents tail).

```text
Game 1: 1 1 0 1 0 0
Game 2: 0 0
Game 3: 1 0 1 1 1 0 0
Game 4: 1 1 1 1 0 0
Game 5: 0 1 1 0 0
Game 6: 1 0 0
Game 7: 1 1 0 1 1 0 0
Game 8: 0 0
Game 9: 1 1 1 0 0
Game 10: 1 0 1 0 1 0 0
```
Answer the following questions using only the provided results. Do not generate any additional games.

(1) *Based on the provided result*, what is the estimated probability that you win more than $\$5$?

\vspace{40pt}

(2) What would happen to the estimated probability in (1) if I simulate the game for 10000 times instead of 10 times?  Choose one.

    (i) The estimate would be the same value as in (1).
    (ii) The estimate would be a larger value than the value in (1).
    (iii) The estimate would be a smaller value than the value in (1).
    (iv) The estimate could be a larger or a smaller value than the value in (1).

(3) Based on the provided result, what is your estimate of the *average* net winning of this game?

\vspace{40pt}

(4) Suppose we want to study the distribution of $L$, the length of the game (i.e., the number of times the coin is flipped when the game ends).  What is the *true* sample space of $L$?

\vspace{40pt}

(5) Based on the provided result, what is the estimated distribution (i.e., probability mass function) of $L$?  Verify that the probability mass function satisfies the two conditions of a probability mass function.

\vspace{20pt}





\newpage

8. (20pt) This question concerns the spread of a disease over five days using a Poisson model. Let $(d_1, d_2, d_3, d_4, d_5)$ denote the total cases on each day. Suppose $d_1=100$ and $R_0=2.8$. Under this model, $d_2$ has a Poisson distribution with parameter $\lambda=d_1\times2.8$, $d_3$ has parameter $\lambda=d_2\times2.8$, and so on.

(1) What is the expected value of $d_2$? What is the variance of $d_2$?

\vspace{20pt}

(2) Express the conditional distributions of $d_3$, $d_4$, and $d_5$ given the preceding day's cases.

\vspace{20pt}

(3) Suppose we want to study the distribution of $d_5$ and estimate:

    (a) the probability that day 5 has fewer than 5000 cases;
    (b) the average number of cases on day 5.

  Describe the four steps of a simulation study without writing any code.

- For one simulation, what are you simulating?  What is an example of a possible outcome?

\vspace{20pt}
- What are the random variable(s) you are recording?

\vspace{20pt}
- Repeat many times; what would your recorded result look like?


\vspace{20pt}
- How do you estimate (a) and (b) in the question using your simulation result?

\vspace{20pt}

(4) Explain how the proportion of simulated values below 5000 would estimate (a), and how the mean of the simulated values would estimate (b).

\vspace{30pt}

(5) Predict the likely spread and shape of the distribution of $d_5$. Explain why uncertainty will increase over the five days.

\vspace{110pt}


- This is a closed-book, closed-notes exam. No reference sheet, computer, phone, calculator, smartwatch, or other electronic device is permitted.




## Written modeling exercise

Suppose the number of new patients arriving at a certain ER in a day, $X$, follows a Poisson distribution with parameter $\lambda_1=30$, and the number of patients the ER can treat, $Y$, follows a Poisson distribution with parameter $\lambda_2=38$. The ER is overcrowded when $X>Y$.

(1) Describe a hand-calculation or simulation design for estimating $P(X>Y)$ without using a computer. What would one trial record?

(2) If one observed day had $X=33$ and $Y=37$, did the ER overcrowd? Explain.

(3) Explain why allowing the rates to vary from day to day could make a Gamma-Poisson model more realistic than fixed Poisson rates.

(4) If $\lambda_1$ has a Gamma distribution with shape 15 and scale 2, what are its mean and variance? If $\lambda_2$ has shape 190 and scale 0.2, what are its mean and variance?


\newpage

9. (12pt) Let $X$ be the number of heads in three tosses of a fair coin.

(1) Write the probability mass function of $X$ in a table.

\vspace{70pt}

(2) Verify that the probabilities are nonnegative and sum to 1.

\vspace{30pt}

(3) Calculate $E(X)$ and explain what the expectation means in context.

\vspace{60pt}


10. (12pt) Suppose you roll three fair dice and record their sum.

(1) Describe one simulation outcome and the single value you would record from that outcome.

\vspace{35pt}

(2) Describe how you would use many repeated outcomes to decide whether a sum of 9 or a sum of 10 is more likely. No code is needed.

\vspace{55pt}

(3) Explain why one roll of the three dice is not enough to decide which sum is more likely.

\vspace{35pt}


11. (12pt) For each scenario, identify the most appropriate distribution and specify its parameter(s).

(1) The number of sixes in 5 rolls of a fair die.

\vspace{25pt}

(2) The number of people asked until the first person who was born in July, if $12\%$ of people were born in July.

\vspace{25pt}

(3) The number of mistakes on a page when mistakes occur at an average rate of 2 per page.

\vspace{25pt}

(4) The number of trials needed to obtain the third success when each trial succeeds with probability $0.7$.

\vspace{35pt}


12. (12pt) A simulation of a gambling game produces the following net winnings after 8 independent games:

$$5,\quad 5,\quad -3,\quad 5,\quad 5,\quad -11,\quad 5,\quad 5.$$

(1) Estimate the probability that the game ends with a win of at least $5$.

\vspace{25pt}

(2) Calculate the sample average of the 8 net winnings.

\vspace{35pt}

(3) Would you expect the estimate based on 8 games to be more or less variable than an estimate based on 10,000 games? Explain.

\vspace{35pt}

(4) Explain why repeating a simulation many times does not guarantee that every simulated result will be different or identical.
